3381.text: In 1Kgs.1.2 no other M-code characteristic is present in the verse's role tags apart from the seeking-act itself (M83); the surrounding vocabulary is untagged narrative detail.

3385.text: In 1Kgs.1.2, the seeking operation is initiated by the servants (party) directed toward finding a young woman for the king (party, the lord/king), i.e. an instrumental search on the king's behalf.

4442.text: In Zech.11.16 H1245 ('seek the young') is used pastorally of a shepherd's duty of care toward vulnerable animals/people - the nuance shifts from literal search toward neglect-implying pastoral responsibility (here notably negated), contrasting with the more neutral seeking of Gen.37.16 and Prov.15.14's intellectual seeking.

4447.text: In Zech.11.16 no other M-code characteristic co-occurs with H1245 in this verse's tag set (the raising-up and destruction/binding words carry M-codes M08/M74/M20/M24 respectively, but these appear on different words, not co-tagged as home-cluster items here) - treating from H1245's own vantage, it stands as the sole M83 instance; other M-codes present (M08, M74, M20, M24, M16) belong to different characteristics but the question scope is restricted to what THIS characteristic's pass records, and since no prior context exists this begins the chain, noting M16 (folly/stupidity, via H1197B-type sense) and M24 (brokenness) surround the neglect motif but relation to seeking is thematic contrast (neglect of shepherding duty) rather than direct semantic overlap.

4452.text: In Zech.11.16 the (negated) seeking operation would be initiated by the shepherd toward the young/lost sheep, but the verse denies this action occurs, marking a failed shepherd-to-flock directional operation.

4988.text: In Esth.2.2 'sought out' shifts H1245 toward administrative procurement/selection (gathering virgins for the king), a bureaucratic sense distinct from personal or religious seeking seen elsewhere -- the impact is depersonalized, institutional searching rather than individual pursuit.

4992.text: In Esth.2.2 the king's young men initiate the seeking-out operation directed toward beautiful young virgins, on behalf of the king.

4996.text: No other M-code characteristic co-occurs meaningfully with H1245 in Esth.2.2 as home-cluster interaction; the seeking-out operates alongside descriptive terms (beauty, youth) but no other M-code party characteristic is present.

5492.text: In 2 Chr 15:13 darash carries its well-attested devotional sense 'seek the Lord' -- this is within the base gloss's own listed sub-sense (1a3, seeking deity in prayer/worship), not a divergence from it; contrast with the necromantic-object occurrences shows the same verb pivoting entirely on its object rather than on any special contextual nuance of the verb form itself.

5495.text: No other M-code characteristic co-occurs in 2 Chr 15:13 alongside the seeking of the Lord; the other tagged items are structural/role tags only.

5498.text: In 2 Chr 15:13 the operation 'put to death' (H4191, role-T3) is directed by the covenant community against whoever fails to seek the Lord; the seeking itself (H1875) is the required act of the individual party directed toward the Lord/God of Israel, and its absence triggers the death-operation against that same individual.

6547.text: In Ps.37.25 'begging' renders baqash for a child seeking bread out of want, a specific nuance of desperate physical need rather than the more common senses of hostile pursuit or devotional seeking found elsewhere (e.g. Ps.27.4, Ps.35.4); the impact here is to underscore God's providence toward the righteous by contrast, since such begging is said never to be observed.

6560.text: Other M-codes present in Ps.37.25: M12 (righteous), M30/M59 (forsaken). Baqash (begging) describes the hypothetical desperate act of a righteous person's child; it stands in negated contrast to being forsaken (M30/M59), illustrating what does NOT happen to the righteous (M12), but does not itself modify those terms.

6572.text: In Ps.37.25, H1245 (begging) is an operation hypothetically initiated by 'his children' (the righteous person's offspring), directed toward obtaining bread — but the verse denies this ever occurs, so the operation is negated rather than actually enacted.

7293.text: Relational scope is broad in principle (any nation or person may seek any deity or authority) but narrow in legitimacy: the Lord invites 'a people... their God' (Isa.8.19) and even nations beyond Israel are said to inquire of the root of Jesse (Isa.11.10), showing an eschatological widening of inclusion; yet within Israel's own covenant, failure to seek excludes one from covenant blessing and even life (2Chr.15.13 'whoever would not seek the Lord... should be put to death'), showing exclusion is covenantal-moral rather than ethnic.

14208.text: How it co-exists: With enforced silence first. "Elihu had waited to speak to Job because they were older than he" (32:4), and "I was timid and afraid to declare my opinion" (32:6). Fear and deference hold the anger in, until the others fall silent; Elihu describes the pressure in bodily terms: "I am full of words; the spirit within me constrains me. Behold, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins ready to burst. I must speak, that I may find relief" (32:18–20). The held anger is felt as pressure in the belly, and speech is its release.

20304.text: Job 15:5 — Eliphaz: "your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty": Eliphaz weighs Job by his words. He opens with *"Should a wise man answer with windy knowledge"* (v2), and charges *"you are doing away with the fear of God and hindering meditation before God"* (v4). Then he names the choice: *"For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty"* (v5). He reads it this way: something inside, iniquity, teaches the mouth; the mouth then chooses a crafty tongue; From that he gives the verdict: *"Your own mouth condemns you, and not I; your own lips testify against you"* (v6).; He takes his evaluation further inside. He moves from the mouth to the heart, eyes and spirit: *"Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash, that you turn your spirit against God and bring such words out of your mouth?"* (v12–13). For Eliphaz, the words show what the heart has chosen.; His grounds for judging are age and tradition: *"Both the gray-haired and the aged are among us, older than your father"* (v10); *"what wise men have told, without hiding it from their fathers"* (v18); His picture of the outcome is the wicked man's end (v20–35).; Set against the book's frame, his charge *"you are doing away with the fear of God"* (v4) runs against the narrator's and the Lord's *"one who feared God"* (1:1, 8). The Lord's verdict in 42:7 is on how Eliphaz spoke of God, not directly on this charge. Still, the man Eliphaz says has chosen the tongue of the crafty is the one the Lord twice calls *"my servant Job"* (42:7–8).

20455.text: 4. Knowing a thought is separate from producing it. 1 Corinthians 2:11 says only "the spirit of that person" knows a person's thoughts, and only God's Spirit knows God's. Separately, God searches and knows human thoughts (Psalm 139:23; 1 Chronicles 28:9; Psalm 94:11; 1 Corinthians 3:20), and so does Jesus (Luke 5:22, 6:8, 11:17; Matthew 9:4, 12:25).: *Caveat:* in 1 Corinthians 2:11 the Strong's number is G3588, the Greek article. The word "thoughts" is supplied by the translation; the Greek says "the things of a person."

20489.text: 9.2 What thoughts are: Design: forming something that does not yet exist. H2803G (19 rows) describes craftsmanship: cherubim "skillfully worked" (Exod 26:1, 31) and "skilled design" (Exod 39:3). The faculty itself is neutral. *Maḥăšāvāh* covers both artistry and plots, and *mᵊzimmāh* covers both "discretion" (Prov 2:11) and "evil devices" (Prov 12:2). What makes a thought good or evil is what it is designed toward.; Reckoning: giving something its value or category. H2803H/J (60 rows): Human misreckoning: Eli "took her to be a drunken woman" (1 Sam 1:13), "we esteemed him stricken" and "we esteemed him not" (Isa 53:3–4), Judah "thought she was a prostitute" (Gen 38:15).; God's reckoning: "he counted it to him as righteousness" (Gen 15:6), "the Lord counts no iniquity" (Ps 32:2), and the nations "accounted as the dust on the scales" (Isa 40:15, 17).; To think is to judge the worth of something, and people can judge wrongly.; Inner speech.; "all his thoughts are, 'There is no God'" (Ps 10:4). The thought is quoted as a sentence.; Hannah "was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved" (1 Sam 1:13).; *Dialogismos* covers both inner reasoning and outward "argument", "quarreling" and "disputing".; "conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse" (Rom 2:15).; Something that affects the body and emotions.; "his thoughts alarmed him; his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together" (Dan 5:6; also 4:19; 5:10; 7:28).; "the cares of my heart" (Ps 94:19), and "haste within me" (Job 20:2).; A divided mind stalls a person: "limping between two different opinions" (1 Kgs 18:21, H5587A).; Creaturely and passing.; "but a breath" (Ps 94:11).; "When his breath departs … on that very day his plans perish" (Ps 146:4).; "futile" (1 Cor 3:20; Rom 1:21).; "striving of heart … striving after wind" (Eccl 2:22; 4:16).; Fully open to God.; "you discern my thoughts from afar" (Ps 139:2); also Ps 139:23; 1 Chr 28:9; "I know their works and their thoughts" (Isa 66:18); Heb 4:12.; Jesus knows people's thoughts (Luke 5:22; 6:8; 9:47; 11:17; Matt 9:4; 12:25).

21222.text: The verb is a close questioning of a captive for what he knows (tree H7592 1a3 'to enquire, enquire of').

21223.text: The questioning is a pursuit: he seeks the names from the captive.

21224.text: What the questioning draws out is the names of the town's leaders, a count of seventy-seven.

21225.text: The answer takes a written form: the names are written down for him.

21226.text: He questions; the young man of Succoth is the one questioned.

21227.text: Gideon has returned from battle and captured the two kings of Midian (Judg 8:12-13), and now captures a young man.

21228.text: He questioned the captured young man about Succoth.

21229.text: He captures a young man, questions him, and has the names of Succoth's leaders written down.

21230.text: The questioning is aimed at those who hold authority in the town.

21231.text: Discovery: what he does with the names is not stated here; the passage shows it (Judg 8:15-16).

21267.text: The verb is a greeting inquiry after a man's state (tree H7592 1a3 'to enquire, enquire of').

21268.text: The asking is a pursuit of word on the Levite's state.

21269.text: What they asked about is the Levite's welfare.

21270.text: The asking comes with their turning aside and coming to his house.

21271.text: The five men ask; the young Levite at Micah's house is the one asked.

21272.text: The five men have passed on to the hill country of Ephraim and come to Micah's house (Judg 18:13), where one of them has spoken of the images (Judg 18:14).

21273.text: The five men asked the young Levite how he fared.

21274.text: They turn aside, come to the Levite's house, and ask after his welfare; then they stand at the gate (Judg 18:16).

21275.text: The asking is a greeting that opens the visit.

21276.text: Discovery: what the men do next at the house is told in the verses that follow (Judg 18:16-17); the passage is needed.

21359.text: Offer here is the ritual or narrated presenting of an offering, a prescribed or reported act with no inner-being operation named by it.

21363.text: Offer here carries no inner-being operation: it is a figure of nature or an outward act of commerce.

21392.text: Old is here the older person toward whom respect, mercy or rebuke is directed; it names the party the act is aimed at, and the act is named by another word of the verse.

21405.text: Old gives the age class of those in whom an inner response is stated: the old are merry, the old men dream dreams.

21419.text: Fury here is the raging of the sea, a wind, a sword, a chariot, a beast or a vine in a figure of nature or war; no inner-being operation is voiced by it.
